title: What is a positive result worth? – Screening accuracy
subtitle: A scroll-driven explanation of sensitivity, specificity and the positive predictive value with 100 people, a playground, the PPV/NPV curves and a guessing game (EN/DE).
course: Psychometrie und psychotherapierelevante Diagnostik (MSc Klinische Psychologie und Psychotherapie)
learning_goals: Explain prevalence, sensitivity and specificity as shares of a group of 100 tested people and read them off a 2×2 table.
Explain the positive predictive value as the share of true cases among plus results, and why the same test yields a low PPV at low prevalence and a high PPV at high prevalence.
Argue why routine screening with a weak test produces mostly false positives, and why interpreting a result requires a prevalence estimate and a test with known measurement properties.
creator: Bitte eintragen
notes: Scroll-driven guided explanation in eleven steps with a landing page that offers the argument or a jump to the game; a pinned picture updates as the text scrolls past it, English by default with a German switch (German uses decimal comma and colon gender forms). Steps 1–8 build the argument with the same 100 figures: 100 people, prevalence (8 have depression), sensitivity (7 of 8 get a plus), specificity (14 of 92 get a plus), the plus group and the PPV with a guess-first moment, the same test at 50 % prevalence, a weak test in routine screening, and two takeaways (a good prevalence estimate; a test with known measurement properties). Each figure carries a + or − badge for the test result; colour is the true condition. Figures move between groups with an animation. Step 9 is a playground with sliders (prevalence 0–100 %, sensitivity and specificity 50–100 %), presets (general population 8 %, GP practice 20 %, psychotherapy practice 50 %; PHQ-9 88/85 after Levis, Benedetti & Thombs 2019; two-question test 96/57 after Whooley et al. 1997; an illustrative excellent test 95/95) and a live 2×2 table with the PPV and NPV arithmetic. Step 10 explains the PPV and NPV curves across prevalence with the current point marked. Step 11 is a six-round guessing game (estimate the PPV for a given setting and test, then check) with the average miss at the end; no score is stored. People are shown as whole figures, rounded within each group; all percentages are calculated with the exact formulas. An appendix lists every formula (cells, sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, likelihood ratios) with a worked example. The Inter typeface is bundled in assets/fonts (SIL Open Font License 1.1, licence file included); the capsule loads no external resources at all. Designed for lecture-hall projection and laptops; no login, no persistence.
